articles.title: This Budget was micro and that was deliberate
articles.text:
It was not a mini Budget, but it was rather small. It might be called the "micro Budget".

Small does not necessarily mean bad, but it clearly falls short of radical action to create a promised new economic model.

A new "theory of growth" was not unveiled as promised by the prime minister Andy Burnham.

It was preamble, roadmap, consultation, perhaps the starter to the main course, which appears to be the PM's 10-year plan next month.

It went unsaid, but the clear stategic aim of Healey's statement was to be the "anti-mini Budget".

This "steady as she goes" predictable fiscal event set out to avoid the aftermath seen following Liz Truss's mini-budget, in which unexpected and unfunded tax cuts spooked the bond and currency markets.

The markets didn't even flicker on Healey's announcement of £65bn of extra borrowing over the next five years - government interest costs have actually fallen since Wednesday, against the backdrop of market turmoil due to the US-Iran war.

The core of the Budget was to get Downing Street through the impacts of the Middle East conflict shock on energy and borrowing costs.

If these pressures prove enduring there are some unpalatable decisions that will have to be grasped within the next year. The can will have to be picked up rather than kicked down the road again.

It buys more time, more "breathing space", as it were, for the government and the prime minister's long-term strategic plans.

On energy, there is some significance to the "cheaper power" mission announced, reshaping what had previously been a focus on clean power.

While still committed to Net Zero, a series of technical changes to powers over levies and renewable auctions, will seek to turn the tide on additional pressures on energy costs.

On devolution, the plan to allow local mayors to keep some extra business rate and income tax revenues, are more radical than expected.

There are trade offs here, but it essentially provides incentives for regional leaders to grow their economies, workforce and tax base, that are normal elsewhere, but have not existed in the UK's very centralised tax system.

How the PM will square other aspects of his "theory of growth" with the chancellor's spending constraints is the other significant challenge.

Can he announce a 10-year plan without detailing the Liverpool to Manchester high speed train line, or a rebirth of some cancelled HS2 lines he championed a year ago?

Away from the long term, the OBR forecast point to a very tricky economic backdrop until the spring, and a trickier spending review, given the need to accommodate the new defence target of 3% of national income by 2030.

The PM's insistence he will not call an election for a year are eminently believable given the risk of 5% inflation and declining household income.

A "focused" Budget at an uncertain time achieved its narrow aim of a bit of "breathing space" for households and also for the government itself.

But the evident gaps in the Budget will need filling in come the PM's upcoming 10-year plan.

articles.title: From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they mean
articles.text:
From the rapidly rising and falling values of Bitcoin to high-profile heists like the hacking of Binance, the world of cryptocurrencies is often in the headlines.

The world's biggest crypto exchange said hackers had gained access to $6.3bn (£4.7bn) worth of digital assets, and while it has frozen about half, many remained in the hands of the thieves.

These stories are full of specialist language that people outside the industry struggle to understand.

So if you're unsure what the blockchain or a crypto echange or even a cryptocurrency itself are, here are some key terms and what they mean.

While many may struggle with the finer points of crypto, pretty much everyone has heard of its most famous product: Bitcoin. But what actually is it?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is to say a type of digital currency. Unlike traditional currencies, Bitcoin is not controlled by centralised financial institutions.

This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom, but it also makes it extremely volatile with it rising and falling in value at the whim of Bitcoin buyers and sellers.

Donald Trump has pledged to make the US the "crypto capital of the world" - backtracking on his previous claim that Bitcoin was a "scam".

Its price topped a much-awaited threshold of $100,000 in December 2024, then rose to $120,000 in July 2025 as US politicians prepared to debate bills to regulate digital assets.

In October 2025, Bitcoin hit an all-time high of around $126,000, buoyed by a continued wave of institutional investment and positive market sentiment. But it has been known to plummet in value just as quickly as it spikes.

In early February 2026, its price dipped below $65,000 to effectively wipe out gains achieved under President Trump.

Against the backdrop of these frequent price fluctuations, speculation continues about the true identity of Bitcoin's mysterious inventor known only as Satoshi Nakamoto.

Blockchain is the technology underpinning all cryptocurrencies, and many related products like non-fungible tokens (NFTs). In essence, it is a virtual spreadsheet on which all the buying and selling of crypto is recorded. They are arranged in blocks linked together in a giant chain - hence the name.

Every cryptocurrency transaction is individually recorded onto the blockchain by a huge network of volunteers verifying its authenticity by using computer programmes.

The incentive to do this for Bitcoin's network is that the first person to validate transactions is rewarded in Bitcoin. This potentially lucrative process, known as mining, is also controversial because of the incredible amount of energy, external used as people the world over race to be the first to successfully update the blockchain.

ETFs are portfolios that let investors bet on multiple assets without having to buy any themselves. Traded on stock exchanges like shares, their value depends on how the overall portfolio performs in real time. They can comprise a combination of gold and silver bullion, for example, or a mix of shares in both technology and insurance companies.

A spot Bitcoin ETF buys the cryptocurrency directly, "on the spot", at its current price, throughout the day.

While some ETFs already contained Bitcoin indirectly, the US approved several spot Bitcoin ETFs in January 2024. This allowed new investors, such as investment management firms like Blackrock and Fidelity, to enter the speculative world of Bitcoin without having to worry about digital wallets or navigating crypto exchanges.

"Stable" is the key word here - this cryptocurrency differs from others as it is intends to be less volatile in value.

This typically works by the price being linked to an existing asset, for instance currencies like the US dollar or pound sterling, which in theory should make them more stable in price than cryptocurrencies that are not backed by assets.

Stablecoins themselves are usually controlled by companies that provide them, with transactions recorded on digital ledgers. While held up by some as the future of finance, high profile price collapses of stablecoins have alerted regulators to risks for investors and prompted scrutiny over their supposed stability.

XRP is a cryptocurrency used by a platform called the XRP Ledger. It was created by the co-founders of financial services company Ripple Labs in 2012 as a cheaper, faster alternative to Bitcoin.

The cryptocurrency has a fixed supply of 100 billion coins, which were created when it launched. Much of it is held by Ripple and periodically released into circulation.

Unlike cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, transactions made using XRP are verified through consensus - whereby the majority of validators on its peer-to-peer network must agree whether or not a transaction is valid before it is added to its blockchain.

This has been credited with allowing many transactions to take place simultaneously, at high speed and low cost - making it appealing to financial institutions or for processes like cross-border payments. But as with other cryptocurrencies, XRP has received regulatory scrutiny and seen sudden, sharp declines in value.

articles.title: Crypto giant Binance hit by hack suspected to be largest in history
articles.text:
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what is thought to be the biggest crypto hack on record.

The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses".

The company said while initial checks suggested an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, "our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach".

Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor.

Cyber-security firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack.

Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record".

AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.

The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen.

The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added.

Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.

The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under its custody.

The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.

Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack.

For the last few years North Korea-linked operatives have focussed on attacking cryptocurrency companies for large thefts of digital tokens.

Western security agencies have previously said stolen funds are used to finance North Korea's nuclear weapons and missile development programs.

The regime has denied any involvement in hacks in the past.

Eric Jardine, Chainalysis' Head of Research, urged every exchange to remain vigilant as the platforms are attractive targets for hackers due to the sheer value of assets.

Binance did not directly respond to BBC questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."

The incident concerns Binance.com - while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US, which provides trading services specifically for American residents - said its platform is not affected by the issue.

articles.title: Eddie Howe to Man Utd? The fans, the finances, the football structure
articles.text:
When Sir Jim Ratcliffe became a co-owner of Manchester United in 2024, much of the narrative centred on his desire to rebuild the club around a British core.

Given the expense of buying homegrown players, and the difficulties Michael Carrick - the first permanent British managerial appointment of the Ineos era - has faced this season, perhaps Ratcliffe is rethinking.

But if Carrick fails to stop the rot and loses his job, United are already considering the merits of appointing another British coach - albeit one who is more experienced.

That Eddie Howe is a contender for a job that remains one of the most high-profile in world football isn't hard to fathom.

Speak to those who have worked alongside Howe and they describe a man whose track record of improving players is a direct result of his relentless approach on the training field.

They will also tell you Howe is someone who places an unwavering importance on the methodology of setting a winning culture.

Howe may lack experience at one of the traditional top-six clubs, but his body of work at Bournemouth and Newcastle is impressive.

Having been appointed Bournemouth boss with the club facing relegation from League Two in January 2009, Howe led them to the Premier League in 2015. He went on to establish the Cherries as a top-flight club before leaving - for a second time - in 2020.

In 2021, Howe was appointed Newcastle manager. He led them from relegation trouble to qualification for the Champions League on two occasions and won the EFL Cup - the club's first trophy in 56 years - in 2025.

Of course, managing Manchester United is an altogether different proposition.

Indeed, Howe's emergence as a potential successor to Carrick has been greeted with negativity in some circles.

Sections of the fanbase have been vocal on social media with their opinion that Howe isn't a big enough name to replace Carrick.

Former United players Paul Scholes and Nicky Butt also fell short of providing their backing to Howe on their podcast, though it is worth pointing out they spoke in favour of the 48-year-old's potential appointment when Ruben Amorim was sacked in January.

Ex-captain Roy Keane is among those to have backed Howe as a possible successor to Carrick, and other former top-flight players - including Darren Bent, Gareth Barry and Jack Wilshere - have also touted him as the man for the job.

Of course, if you look hard enough you'll find voices for and against every potential manager, and it will be up to United chief executive Omar Berrada, sporting director Jason Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell to weigh up how they proceed.

Their first decision will be what happens with Carrick, and Saturday's match against Chelsea is likely to have a bearing on how United move forward.

If Carrick does depart, finances will inevitably be a factor.

The former Middlesbrough boss and his staff will need to be paid up before United even get to factoring in the monetary commitment towards their next head coach.

While the details of Howe's agreement with Newcastle when he left in the summer remain confidential, it is understood that as things stand any club or national team would be required to pay a seven-figure compensation fee to the Magpies.

Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that Newcastle - with a view to protecting themselves against Howe walking straight into another club - reached an agreement over a compensation structure that decreases over time.

It is understood that figure started at £6m but has already reduced by half.

The compensation payments have an expiry date - understood to be before the end of the season - at which point he can be appointed for nothing.

Of course, in an industry in which astronomical figures are the norm, the prospect of paying a maximum of £3m for Howe may not be too problematic.

That said, given the amount Manchester United have spent on hiring and firing managers in recent years, it is understandable if Berrada and Wilcox want to keep costs down.

Howe is an obvious contender for the Manchester United job, just as he would be if the England head coach's position became available.

Whether he is offered it or not will give a clear indication about the path United are going down.

Director of football Jason Wilcox is thought to favour the 48-year-old, with director of recruitment Christopher Vivell preferring former Bayern Munich and Germany coach Julian Nagelsmann.

Ultimately, their recommendations will be assessed by chief executive Omar Berrada, with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and co-chairs Joel and Avram Glazer having the final say.

It is not completely clear where the negativity about Howe moving to Old Trafford comes from, other than Wilcox being targeted by Manchester United fans during the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth.

In the current managerial climate, few managers get the chance to build a body of work at one club over a number of years as, for instance, Sir Alex Ferguson did at Aberdeen before he moved south in November 1986.

There is clearly a general disillusionment among the club's matchgoing fans around the football decisions taken since Ratcliffe bought his minority stake in early 2024, but Erik ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick have all been backed.

Some say no manager can succeed at United with the structure as it is, and it is clear whoever is in charge needs to mould together a squad bought by six permanent managers, most of whom have differing playing styles.

articles.title: Jamie Carragher sued: Aston Villa to take legal action against pundit over 'unacceptable insults'
articles.text:
Aston Villa say they will initiate legal action against Jamie Carragher over what the club branded as "unacceptable insults".

Posting on their social media on Friday, Villa released a statement signed by their chairman Nassef Sawiris accusing Carragher of insulting the Premier League side and its fans.

It added the club would "not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football".

Speaking on the Stick to Football podcast, Carragher attracted criticism from Villa fans by suggesting their manager Unai Emery would be interested in becoming Manchester United's head coach.

Michael Carrick's position at United is hanging in the balance after a dismal start to the campaign and Carragher said "Aston Villa will never be Manchester United".

"Surely he would want that opportunity to manage a giant again," Carragher said.

"There is a chain in football, whether you like it or not.

"So Real Madrid will take Manchester United's best player, they did it with [Cristiano] Ronaldo.

"And there will be teams below Aston Villa, and they'll take their players or manager, so shut the [expletive] up Aston Villa fans. Aston Villa will never be Manchester United."

Carragher, a football pundit for works for Sky Sports and American broadcaster CBS, has already commented on the backlash he received after he told the fans to shut up.

"It was a joke after the stick Villa fans have given me over saying Emery may fancy joining Man Utd," Carragher said on social media.

"I hope these clown clips show me praising Emery/Villa like I have done for years & saying how pleased I was you won [the 2026 Europa League] in Istanbul."

On the Overlap Daily, Carragher went into more detail.

"I just think Unai Emery is the best manager in the league and if you're Man Utd you're thinking 'what's the best we can get?'. I'm not saying he'll go - I'm just saying if it was me I'd ask the question," said Carragher.

"Certain managers are good at certain clubs and that's Emery. He reminds me of Rafa [Benitez]. I think your own ego if someone said 'that's your level' would say 'no I'm not'. That was my point.

"It's grew arms and legs. I ended up telling them to [expletive] which maybe I shouldn't have done but it was all in jest because they've been all over my social timeline. I was saying [expletive] off my socials."

articles.title: Beat Luke Littler: Farron Sherrock upsets world champion to claim £501,000 prize
articles.text:
Fallon Sherrock defeated reigning world champion Luke Littler in one leg of darts on Friday to win £501,000.

Broadcast live globally on Netflix, Beat Luke Littler featured a host of amateur players taking on world number one Littler in a one-leg face-off at Manchester Central.

Players could not be members of the PDC Tour, meaning Sherrock, who became the first female player to beat a male opponent at the PDC World Championship on her way to the last 32 in December 2019, was allowed to compete.

After Littler had defeated 14 amateurs, some as young as 14, he was always going to have a tough task against 32-year-old Sherrock, a player who has won 21 times on the PDC Women's Series.

She had been closest to the bull to start first and hit a 180, only the third maximum of the night, before taking out double 20 to clinch the prize.

Sherrock, whose son Rory was among the crowd, said: "It's insane, I can't put it into words of what it means, especially having Rory here - it's his first time at anything and he has seen me win.

"It's a great moment and I will memorise this forever. Give me an opportunity and I will take it every time. I'm really proud of myself, I rise to the occasion."

Nineteen-year-old Littler, who has won the PDC World Championship in both the past two events, said: "Brilliant, that's what one person had to do - win the bull and go out in 15 [darts] and that's what she did, world class."

The packed crowd in Manchester was in boisterous mood with many fans in fancy dress, but this was darts with a difference.

There had been 25,000 applicants who had entered the competition.

The first stage saw players have to get down from 501 in 24 darts or less, with those successful then facing a three-person interview panel, including 16-time world champion Phil Taylor, PDC president Barry Hearn and darts television pundit Laura Turner.

Twenty players were due to play at the event. Sixteen were selected outright, while the eight most experienced players were paired off, with Netflix viewers voting on which one should be able to compete.

Sherrock was in the vote against Germany's Jarod Becker, but collected 75% of the votes to get the chance to face Littler.

She had picked up £25,000 for reaching round three of the PDC World Championship at Alexandra Palace seven years ago after beating Ted Evetts and Mensur Suljovic before losing to Chris Dobey.

Her achievement saw her nicknamed 'The Queen of the Palace' and she was also awarded an MBE for her services to darts in 2023.

Sherrock's victory over Littler meant the event immediately ended, meaning the five remaining amateurs were unable to get their shot at the £501,000 prize.

While Sherrock was celebrating, Ireland's 'Fierce' Pearse Mackle, a 21-year-old university student from County Cavan, was left wondering what could have been.

Mackle, who competes on PDC's Development Tour, was the eighth competitor and failed to hit a match-winning bullseye, instead finding the nine, and his life-changing moment came and went.

He was the only other player, apart from Sherrock, to cause Littler a fright.

For most of the night, Littler cruised through the competition as he went in search of the £501,000, which he had said he would donate to charity.

With former England footballer Gary Lineker hosting and with comedian Lee Mack and television presenter Richard Osman joining Turner as part of the punditry team, this was a night to bring darts to a new audience.

The first challenger was 16-year-old Kasey Smith from Manchester, but Littler showed he was in no mood to mess about, hitting treble 20s against her with his first two darts on his way to an easy win.

Some of Littler's opponents had never played a competitive game of darts, although everyone was keen to make the most of the experience.

With John McDonald, who retired as the main PDC master of ceremonies after the 2026 World Championship final, announcing the players before their elaborate walk-ons, this was a fun event, although most players came nowhere near beating Littler.

But there were still entertaining moments. Fourteen-year-old Jayden Walker, a year 10 pupil from Dorset, threw off a school blazer and tie to reveal his darts outfit and, as the third-highest ranked player, threatened to cause a huge shock.

But Littler raised his game when he needed to, hitting a maximum 180 followed by a 158 checkout, the highest of the night, to defeat his fellow teenager in only 12 darts.

Taylon Forrester, 18, described himself as a "binman who works with his dad" and he jumped out of a dumpster on his way to the oche.

Other entrants included Zac Spain, a jockey from Melbourne, Australia, Frenchman Theodore Wallich, who dubbed himself the 'Moustache Kid', 57-year-old Mark Pooke, another 14-year-old in Makinley Cooper-Johnson and Will Kemp, back playing after a heart attack earlier this year.

But Sherrock, whose participation in the competition had been questioned because of her past achievements in the sport, was the real winner, even if she had been described by Lineker as a "hairdresser from Milton Keynes".

With Littler on stage for more than two hours, he inevitably tired with his standard dropping and Sherrock was the one to take advantage, winning in a 15-dart leg in match number 15.

Hearn reappeared to present Sherrock with a huge cheque for her life-changing victory to end a surreal night of action.

articles.title: United States 12-55 England: Red Roses return to winning ways
articles.text:
United States (7) 12

Tries: Rogers, Zackary Cons: Vogel

Tries: Moloney-MacDonald (4), Jones, Venner, Field, Feaunati, Kabeya Cons: Sing (2), Harrison (3)

England's Red Roses returned to winning ways, but without entirely vanquishing doubts over their position at the top of the women's game, as they saw off a spirited United States in New Jersey.

England started steadily enough with wing Claudia Moloney-MacDonald crossing twice in the first 12 minutes, her second coming via a looping mis-pass from fly-half Holly Aitchison.

However the United States, who were obliterated 69-7 in the opening match of England's march to the Rugby World Cup last year, stuck in the contest far longer than they did that day in Sunderland.

The sixth-ranked underdogs were still snarling deep into the second half with one thunderous hit from Alev Kelter, hoisting and dumping England captain Meg Jones, rallying her team.

Ultimately Moloney-MacDonald ran in four tries as England exploited space out wide, but their final performance of the WXV Global Series, after two losses to Canada over the previous fortnight, will give head coach John Mitchell plenty to ponder before the start of their Women's Six Nations title defence in April.

The United States claimed a second try with the final play of the match as Kate Zackary dived over around the fringes at the end of a surge that summed up their determination.

While Mitchell will undoubtedly take positives – Holly Aitchison's play-making and Maud Muir's all-action performance among them – he has plenty on his to-do list.

Top will be to tune up his team's set-piece solidity and attacking fluency.

England suffered at the line-out early on, unable to fire up their rolling maul from two promising attacking positions before being shoved back over their own line, only for Kathryn Treder's try to be ruled out for a obstruction call.

The scrum was also, initially at least, more closely contested than expected.

Muir was pinged as the experienced Hope Rogers grappled for set-piece supremacy.

And, all the while, the hosts were making headway at the gainline, buying territory with brute physicality - an aspect of the game which is usually England's trademark.

The United States got their reward as Rogers burrowed beneath Maddie Feaunati for a short-range score that sparked lasting celebrations.

Jones went over after full-back Emma Sing hit a good line to restore a 10-point lead by the break, but the stats below the scoreboard favoured the United States with the hosts enjoying more territory and possession and making more metres with the ball in hand at the interval.

Moloney-MacDonald's third and fourth scores soon after the restart put England 20 points clear and the outcome out of doubt.

The United States, who came into the match on the back of five-match winning run that includes successes over Ireland and South Africa, hung tough however.

While England's endurance and depth told, with Hannah Botterman impressing off the bench, Ellie Kildunne weaving up from backfield on her introduction, the tide turning in the scrum and four tries scored in the final quarter, the hosts' energy was impressive.

Even with replacement prop Mona Lisa Tupou being sent to the sin bin for a scrum infringement, their resistance and physicality stayed high and was rewarded with Zackary's late score.

With both the attendance and the playing surface appearing patchy at the 25,000-capacity Sports Illustrated Stadium, organisers will hope to have a more impressive platform in place by the time the Women's Rugby World Cup is held stateside in 2033.

articles.title: Mexico City Grand Prix practice result: Max Verstappen says Liam Lawson collision 'not very smart'
articles.text:
Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson were both given one-place grid penalties for an incident in which they collided in Friday practice at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Verstappen accused Lawson of "not very smart behaviour" and trying to "drive me off the track at the hairpin" as the two disputed the same piece of track during the session.

The four-time champion and the New Zealander clashed in the stadium section towards the end of the lap, with the two cars hitting each other side-on after running through three corners side by side.

Race stewards decided that both had been at fault for the incident and took the unusual step of issuing a sporting penalty for an infringement in practice.

The FIA stewards report said that Verstappen was preparing for a flying lap and Lawson on a "cool-down" lap after a timed lap "preparing for another push lap".

It added: "The drivers of both cars behaved in a manner that was considered unacceptable by the stewards."

It said: "Both drivers admitted the moves were unnecessary and 'clumsy'."

Verstappen, speaking before the stewards' verdict, said: "Maybe not very smart behaviour what he was trying to do there.

"At the end of the day it is not going to change my weekend, but if I were him I would act a little smarter and when you're fighting for your seat it's not very smart behaviour."

Lawson is one of three drivers competing for two seats at Racing Bulls, Red Bull's junior team, next year, alongside current team-mate Arvid Lindblad and Bulgarian Formula 2 front-runner Nikola Tsolov, who drove for Racing Bulls in first practice on Friday.

Verstappen has an influential position within the Red Bull organisation as their star driver.

The Dutchman added: "When he saw me coming, he suddenly started to accelerate. I don't know what was going through his head, that he wanted to drive me off the track in the hairpin.

"That's not very sensible behaviour from someone in his position, to pick a fight with me."

Lawson was Verstappen's team-mate for two races at the start of 2025 before being dropped back down to the Racing Bulls junior team after disappointing performances.

He had a second spell alongside Verstappen for three races this year as a substitute for regular driver Isack Hadjar after the Frenchman broke his wrist. Lawson acquitted himself more effectively on his second time in the senior team.

Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane said: "One word - unnecessary. And I say that of both of them. I haven't heard what Max has said. I'm sure he's got his opinions and I'm sure Liam has his opinion. But mine is, it's just not needed and they can both do better."

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc headed McLaren's Lando Norris in the times. Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli, who is poised to clinch his first world title on Sunday, was fourth fastest behind team-mate George Russell.

Antonelli's expected coronation is the main event of the weekend - only a victory by Russell or Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton can theoretically stop Antonelli becoming champion on Sunday. Even then, Antonelli only needs ninth place if Russell wins and 10th if Hamilton does.

Leclerc, who topped both sessions on Friday, was 0.103 seconds quicker than Norris, with Russell just 0.003secs further adrift.

Antonelli was 0.217secs off the pace, and ahead of the Red Bulls of Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar.

Leclerc's team-mate Lewis Hamilton was 11th overall after stopping on track with a technical problem before completing his qualifying simulation runs on the soft tyre.

"I was feeling really good in the car," said Hamilton. "It's just my luck.

"We did a really good job of getting the set-up in a better place. It's just really unfortunate. I think we're really competitive this weekend as a team and then didn't get to do the long run so I have no idea. It's really difficult to overtake here."

Russell said: "Ferrari are looking strongest at the moment, Leclerc didn't properly finish his lap. Lewis has the issue. We expected on this sort of circuit for them to perform best but Q3 as it stands can go any way."

Behind Hadjar, Racing Bulls duo Arvid Lindblad and Lawson sandwiched Pierre Gasly's Alpine, while McLaren's Oscar Piastri completed the top 10.

On the race-simulation runs later in the session, Leclerc again appeared to be the fastest, but the top four teams were all very closely matched and there looked to be little to choose between the soft and medium tyres.

The runs suggested a one-stop is the most likely strategy on Sunday and overtaking will be difficult because of the challenge of staying close to another car when overheating is such a challenge in the thin air at the 2,200m altitude of Mexico City.

The first session was marked by 10 of the 11 teams running 'rookie' drivers in their cars.

One of them was Cadillac's Colton Herta, who the team are considering promoting to a race seat in place of Valtteri Bottas next season.

Initially, the team felt his running in Mexico had given him enough points under the F1 system to earn a 'superlicence', which is required to race in F1.

But further investigation by governing body the FIA revealed the American nine-time Indycar race winner is still one point short and will have to complete one further practice session this year to secure his licence.

The team plan to do that before the end of the season at one of the forthcoming races.

articles.title: South Africa vs Australia: Hosts set up epic finale - what do stats and history suggest could happen?
articles.text:
Third Test, Cape Town (day four of five)

South Africa 329 & 387: Mulder 115, Rickelton 101

Australia 429: Inglis 102; Harmer 4-104

Australia need 288 to win

A gripping series has the finale it deserves.

Having effectively began day four on 40-4, South Africa batted on and on against Australia in Cape Town to move from a position where defeat looked likely to one where a series victory is a real possibility.

In being bowled out for 387 in the final over - with Ryan Rickelton making 101 and Wiaan Mulder last man out for a brilliant 115 - South Africa set the tourists a target of 288 for victory.

WinViz - the tool analysts CricViz use to predict such results - gives the hosts a 54% chance of victory.

If only things were that simple…

Australia's target is such that should they chase it on day five, it would be the second-highest fourth-innings chase in the 62 previous Tests on this famous ground.

The highest? That's a good omen for Australia.

They chased 331 for a four-wicket win in an epic Test against the Proteas in 2002, when Ricky Ponting hit a brilliant 100 not out.

There have been five other scores above 288 in the fourth innings at Newlands - all of which were made in defeats or when salvaging a draw.

For much of the afternoon and evening sessions, as Australia's bowlers tired, this surface appeared flat enough to score.

When Rickelton and Mulder applied themselves, few opportunities were created. They were able to progress to their third and fourth Test centuries respectively.

It took a run out to end Rickelton's knock, after which Marco Jansen pulled to deep square leg and Gerald Coetzee was also run out - three dismissals down to batter error in a collapse of 4-61, which left South Africa nine down and 251 runs ahead.

That Mulder and number 11 Kagiso Rabada flogged 36 before the close, suggested run-scoring is not impossible.

None of those late runs were made under the pressure of a chase, however.

The wicket of Simon Harmer in the final session, bowled shouldering arms by a ball from Nathan Lyon which turned back sharply showed the difficulty ahead.

Harmer dismissed Travis Head, Marnus Labuschagne, Josh Inglis and Alex Carey in Australia's first innings - all recognised batters.

The 37-year-old Essex legend, who once considered playing for England, will be crucial.

As ever in such scenarios, the pitch will play its part.

The PitchViz rating - CricViz's way of assessing the difficulty of a surface - jumped to 6.6 in the final session, comfortably the highest (thus most difficult) rating of the Test.

After settling down in the morning, the ball, as would be expected as a Test progresses, was turning significantly more in the final session than at any point across the previous four days.

Interestingly, however, South Africa's false shot percentage was just 11% across day four, a drop from 18% on day three.

Uneven bounce has not yet been a factor but one ball to Rickelton shortly after tea also shot low.

articles.title: Jack Grealish dropped by Everton: The future for ex-England winger
articles.text:
When Jack Grealish breezed back into Everton in his white Lamborghini one hour before the end of this summer's transfer deadline, the excitement among supporters and the player himself was clearly evident.

Grealish's previous spell on loan from Manchester City had been cut short by a serious foot injury, but the 31-year-old had produced enough moments of excitement to make his return to the Finch Farm training base a rare moment of joy amid a miserable summer in the transfer market.

When Grealish finally left in the early hours - with the deal done, every autograph signed and every selfie posed for - it was a sort of homecoming for an everyman personality Everton fans had come to regard as one of their own.

This was a move with a lot riding on it - for Everton manager David Moyes, who had been left with only 18 senior players after a botched transfer window, and especially for Grealish, whose exile from City at the start of the final year of his contract confirmed his banishment.

Now, Grealish's future and Everton's faith in him, has reached a defining moment.

Grealish's exclusion from Everton's squad before the Carabao Cup tie at home to Newcastle was publicly described as "a breach of club discipline".

Specifically, it was a failure to turn up for training on Monday, leaving the talented maverick - who was Britain's first £100m footballer when he signed for City from Aston Villa in summer 2021 - facing another rebuild in his career.

Everton's decision to go public before the game with the reasons for Grealish's absence emphasised the seriousness of his transgression.

The fall-out means this now looks increasingly like Grealish's 'now or never' moment, because failure at Everton will surely mark a downward spiral from the top echelons of the Premier League.

Everton do not regard this week's misdemeanour as marking the proverbial 'Last Chance Saloon' for Grealish. Moyes does not have enough players at his disposal to make rapid outcasts of potential game-changers.

But it increases the pressure on the former England forward to win back the faith of fans who love his obvious enjoyment of life and the magic he has shown he can produce.

Moyes will hope it is a harsh lesson learned, because Everton now have even more to play for, given Wembley has suddenly come into view in the Carabao Cup.

BBC Sport believes there have been occasional time-keeping issues with Grealish in the past, but nothing on this scale from a personality regarded as a hard trainer who, in general, keeps himself in good condition.

Grealish has held talks with those in authority at Everton, where it is sure to have been made crystal clear there must be no repeat, certainly not under a strict disciplinarian such as Moyes, and he must now attempt to be rehabilitated back into the squad.

The inevitable decision to punish Grealish, taken at a high level within the club but with input and full support from Moyes, leaves him at the crossroads.

That is especially the case because Everton gave arguably their best performance of the season to beat Newcastle United 3-1 and set up a quarter-final at League Two Fleetwood Town, conquerors of Premier League champions Arsenal in the last round.

And it was done with the more dynamic style of 20-year-old Tyrique George playing on the left flank, which Grealish might have been expected to occupy.

Moyes was guarded after the game and instead preferred to focus on a vital victory.

"You probably know I'm not going to give any details. It's a club decision and I support it. It's something I don't want to speak too much about," he said.

"The one thing about Everton is that they have got real good values. All the players stand behind it and accept the values, on the pitch and off the pitch, and I think the players did a good job.

"It is a small squad, but we are doing our best to keep challenging. We are not accepting any excuses for anything and I think the players are doing a great job. There was a humility about us."

The words were not specifically aimed at Grealish, but they might as well have been from a manager who will have been bitterly disappointed and angry about his transgression.

Moyes and Grealish formed a close relationship from virtually their first moment of contact in August 2025, the latter saying: "As soon as I spoke to the manager, I knew there was only one place that I wanted to go and that was Everton."

And Grealish, a key figure when Manchester City won the Treble of Premier League, FA Cup and Champions League in 2023, played his part until sustaining a foot fracture that ended his season in Everton's 1-0 win at his former club Aston Villa in January.

Grealish's happiness with life at Everton was illustrated when he decided against returning to City, continuing his rehabilitation at Finch Farm rather than going back to Etihad Stadium.

Everton weighed up a second loan deal to bring Grealish back carefully, with his injury, finances and - to a certain extent - his character all entering the equation before Moyes decided to move again for a player who insisted Merseyside was the only place he wanted to be.

Moyes was also juggling very limited options as owners The Friedkin Group appeared to back away from serious squad strengthening as they prepared to put the club up for sale.

Grealish's form this season has been underwhelming, failing to score or create an assist in eight appearances - two of those at City before returning to Everton - while his tendency to slow play down is at odds with the usual tempo Moyes requires from his team.

Moyes' fury will have increased because Grealish, who missed Saturday's loss at Arsenal through "illness", is part of a paper-thin squad that simply cannot carry passengers or have players ruling themselves out through needless ill-discipline.

There will be frustration too, as Grealish is a hugely popular within Everton's dressing room as well as with staff in every area of the club. He has been described as "a lad with a heart of gold, kind and charming, who actually loves being here".

This was illustrated when he recently made a £10,000 donation to a GoFundMe page for Everton fan Leon Skapars, 36, a father of three who has been diagnosed with cancer.

The family are raising money in a search for treatment options, and Skapars' wife Crystal said: "In that moment, Jack gave our whole family something we desperately needed, hope. What he has done for our family is something we will never forget. It makes us feel incredibly emotional."

Grealish also appeared to present awards at the Daily Mirror's 'Pride Of Britain' event recently, saying: "Footballers are classed as heroes - but these are the real heroes."

On Friday, Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca refused to discuss Grealish's actions at Everton, but did praise his character.

Maresca said: "It's not correct to talk about Jack in this moment, first of all because he is an Everton player and secondly because I don't have all the information.

"I still think he is a good guy and has a big heart."

In April, Grealish extended his role as principal ambassador to Special Olympics Great Britain for a further three years, having first joined in 2022.

Grealish marked the occasion by hosting five of the 10 Special Olympics GB athletes who completed the London Marathon at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium, surprising the athletes with a VIP experience, a stadium tour and spending time with them pitchside.

Those at Everton also regard Grealish as one of the first to engage with their community programme at Finch Farm, as well as meeting with the Everton in the Community Down Syndrome team.

Grealish often talks about the inspiration he takes from his sister Hollie, who has cerebral palsy.

He has, however, hit the headlines in less welcome circumstances over the years, and this latest incident ushered in more.

In April, Grealish was pictured asleep at a Manchester rooftop bar surrounded by drinks. It was a scene that is certainly not against the law but was at best unwise, especially with ever-present phone cameras around and the fact he was in rehabilitation from injury.

In March 2020, he was fined by his club Aston Villa and apologised publicly after breaking lockdown guidelines during the pandemic after leaving his house to visit a friend.

In November 2020, he admitted two counts of careless driving relating to two incidents in which a Citroen van and a Mercedes were damaged.

And yet, speak to most people in football - certainly at Everton - and the character references are unfailingly glowing about his outgoing personality and kind-hearted gestures, making his breach of discipline even more painful for his many admirers.

But after this latest setback, Grealish is running out of time and opportunities to justify that continued support.

articles.title: The Prem: Bristol 16-22 Exeter: Leicester dominate Bristol to go top
articles.text:
Tries: Rees-Zammit Cons: Williams Pens: Williams 3

Tries: Steward, Radwan, Hassell-Collins, Blamire Cons: Searle

Leicester took maximum points to go top of the Prem before the rest of the weekend fixtures with a 22-16 win away at Bristol.

Tries from Freddie Steward and Adam Radwan put Tigers in the driving seat after a sublime score from Louis Rees-Zammit had given Bristol an early lead.

Ollie Hassell-Collins extended Leicester's advantage to 17-7 after the break and while James Williams' two penalties closed the gap, Jamie Blamire drove over for the visitors' fourth to all-but seal victory.

But with Billy Searle missing three conversions, Leicester were not as far clear as they could have been and a third penalty from Williams closed the gap to six points to give Bristol hope in the final minutes.

Yet the hosts had to settle for a single losing bonus point as the Tigers did enough to see out the match and leapfrog Gloucester at the summit, with the Cherry and Whites set to play Northampton on Saturday (17:30 GMT).

Both sides came into the game evenly matched with three wins apiece before the autumn international break, and it was the hosts who struck first through a world-class Rees-Zammit try.

The Welsh wing side-stepped his way free and then skipped out of a tackle to run clear and dive under the posts for his fifth Prem try of the season.

Leicester responded, stealing possession to attack on the counter and Searle neatly kicked the ball out wide, where Tigers had numbers, for Steward to score in the corner on his 100th Prem start.

There were chances for more tries at either end as Fitz Harding was held up over the line for Bristol, while the excellent Ollie Chessum got the ball down for Leicester, but it was chalked off for a knock-on beforehand.

Rees-Zammit came inches away from doubling his tally as he shrugged his way out of a tackle and chased down his own chip, only for Tom Whiteley to expertly deny him.

But the momentum shift came just after the half-hour mark when Bristol indiscipline saw them down to 13 thanks to two high tackles in three minutes, with Matias Moroni and Tom Jordan sent to the bin.

With space open everywhere Tigers capitalised and Radwan sprinted sublimely from nowhere to dot down a kick that caught Bristol napping.

After spilling a catch before half-time that would have seen him score, Hassell-Collins got his try the other side of the break, this time easily collecting Searle's crossfield kick in acres of space to stretch the lead to 17-7.

Williams' penalty narrowed the gap and his second eventually brought Bristol within four points with 20 minutes to go.

But Leicester struck again to add the bonus-point score as Blamire walked over at the back of a driving maul.

Still, three missed conversions meant Leicester were not yet home and dry and Williams' third penalty with seven minutes to go set up a tense finale, but Leicester held firm to end the first block of Prem games on a high.

articles.title: Vienna Open: Alexander Zverev thrashes Arthur Fery to reach Vienna Open semis
articles.text:
Alexander Zverev marked his rise to world number one with a dominant victory over Britain's Arthur Fery to reach the semi-finals of the Vienna Open.

The German top seed, who is set to replace Jannik Sinner at the summit of the men's rankings, needed just 58 minutes to secure a comprehensive 6-0 6-2 win.

Fery did not look at his best throughout the encounter after receiving treatment on his leg near the end of his last-16 win over Lorenzo Musetti on Thursday.

The match was a repeat of the pair's Wimbledon semi-final this summer, which Zverev won in straight sets to end Fery's remarkable run.

"I think Arthur is a bit of a different opponent than I had yesterday. He doesn't have the same firepower, but he plays tactically extremely well," said Zverev.

"I know the score was 6-0 6-2, but he should not put himself down too much. It is his first year on the Tour and he is doing amazing things."

Like at Wimbledon, Fery upset the odds to reach the last eight in Vienna by beating former world number five Musetti, but the 24-year-old was outclassed by Zverev.

Zverev dropped only six points on serve in the match, while bringing up nine break points against Fery, converting five of them.

The German is aiming for his third title this year after winning the French Open and US Open.

He has taken advantage of injuries to Carlos Alcaraz and Sinner this year to leapfrog them in the rankings, becoming the second German to reach the top of the men's game after Boris Becker in 1991.

Zverev will face Australian fifth seed Alex de Minaur or Italy's Matteo Berrettini in the last four.

In the other semi-final, Spanish second seed Alcaraz will face Russian third seed Daniil Medvedev.

Seven-time Grand Slam-winner Alcaraz beat American seventh seed Tommy Paul 6-4 7-6 (7-2) in his quarter-final.

Medvedev triumphed over France's Adrian Mannarino 6-2 6-3 in his last-eight tie - a victory which seals the 30-year-old's place in the season-ending ATP Finals.

It will be Medvedev's seventh time appearing at the finals as he joins the already-qualified Zverev, Alcaraz and Ben Shelton.

At the Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo, world number one Elena Rybakina withdrew from her quarter-final tie against Leylah Fernandez with a neck injury.

Rybakina's withdrawal comes one day after she secured the year-end women's singles number one ranking.

Fernandez, who received a walkover, will face Russia's Kamilla Rakhimova in the last-four.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Set up to fail? Where England's World Cup campaign went wrong
articles.text:
As Mikey Lewis darted over for a late try in a desperate - and almost certainly fruitless - points chase against Papua New Guinea, the obituaries were already being written for England's Men's Rugby League World Cup campaign.

Much earlier on Friday, England's women had lacked the power and nous to overcome Samoa, losing 24-6 in a match that decided who went through to the semi-finals.

England's men actually won their game - 34-12 - but it was nowhere near the margin of victory required. Their elimination will be confirmed on Sunday unless Tonga beat Samoa by more than 46 points.

And so the likelihood is that for the first time in World Cup history, neither England's men nor their women will feature in the last four.

For the men, that ends a run that began with Great Britain at the first tournament in 1954.

The disappointment will only reinforce the idea that English rugby league needs a serious period of introspection - as well as significant investment to keep pace with the game in the southern hemisphere.

But there have been other factors to trouble England at this World Cup, hosted by Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea at short notice after France pulled out for financial reasons.

Even before a ball was kicked, the men were faced with a sense of impending doom - brought on by injuries, shambolic travel arrangements and a bizarre format that had England facing immediate jeopardy with a testing opener against Tonga.

The northern hemisphere game has deep-rooted problems, and seems to be stuck in stasis when compared with the thriving NRL.

England had a record of being a major player at World Cups - having reached two finals and a further four semi-finals at the past six tournaments.

But when last autumn's 3-0 Ashes series defeat by Australia prompted the departure of head coach Shaun Wane, his successor was handed a near-impossible task.

Brian McDermott was appointed in April. Given just six months to prepare, the former Leeds Rhinos head coach had no mid-season international to work on a plan. Based in Australia because of his role as Gold Coast Titans assistant coach, he relied on virtual meetings to connect with his prospective squad and staff.

Four on-field sessions were planned in Australia before the World Cup. But only two were completed in full after his UK-based players were subjected to a 48-hour journey to Perth that left them exhausted - a situation McDermott compared to Planes, Trains and Automobiles, the 1987 road-trip comedy starring Steve Martin and John Candy.

It was a shambolic way to prepare for a pivotal opener against Tonga - one that always had the potential to consign the defeated team to an early elimination.

Following that 30-12 loss, McDermott said: "You give me another two or three weeks preparation or another couple of games of preparation leading into the tournament and I'd be really excited."

With the tournament organisers planning travel itineraries for the teams involved, any post-World Cup debrief ought to examine how that situation was allowed to occur.

It would have made more sense for England's opener to be against France - the only other team in the men's tournament made up largely of northern hemisphere-based players.

Wakefield Trinity's historic triumph may have delivered a wonderful sign-off story to the Super League season but it delivered another conundrum around England's squad selection.

Had McDermott known prior to 5 October that none of the Wakefield players in his thinking would be available, could arrangements have been made for his UK-based players to travel to Australia earlier?

In the end, only three of the 14 England-based players in the squad (George Williams, Matty Ashton and Ben Currie) participated in the Super League Grand Final on 3 October.

"If we come together next year as a group, we will be further down the track and we don't need to start from scratch," McDermott added.

"Bear in mind when we landed in Perth on the Friday [9 October], we are starting... like we didn't know each other.

"We were putting things in place about who we are as a group, what it means to us, how we are going to play, how we are going to attack and how we are going to defend. There's been a ton of work gone on."

While much of the pre-tournament noise centred on the omission of Jake Connor and England's long-running halves debate, very little focus was given to a decimated forward pack and other notable absentees.

Prior the first match, McDermott recounted Australia prop Tino Fa'asuamaleaui's admiration for the strength of the English pack during last year's Ashes series.

England's ability to front up had also previously been talked up by Kangaroos boss Kevin Walters.

Yet McDermott had few of those same players at his disposal.

Matty Lees' season-ending injury in May was not only a blow for St Helens but also robbed England of a key enforcer, one who had previously shown he could stand up to the physicality of a powerhouse Tonga front row.

With second-rower Mike McMeeken and prop Caleb Hamlin-Uele unavailable, Morgan Smithies withdrawing from the squad injured and a calf complaint taking Morgan Knowles out of the equation for the encounter against Tonga, England were left short in that area.

That is before you even get to options such as Sydney Roosters' Billy Smith, Wigan's Jake Wardle and Leeds Rhinos duo Ash Handley and Mikolaj Oledzki, all absent through injury.

And when England had to chase the scoreboard after their defeat by Tonga - while hoping results elsewhere went in their favour - it left them in trouble.

They failed to get the numbers on the board they needed against Papua New Guinea. McDermott acknowledged that it left him and his players waiting for the inevitable.

"It feels like we lost the game," he said. "We won and, in any circumstances I would be really proud but I think something remarkable is going to have to happen now for us to go through.

"We've made massive strides together in such a short period of time, in difficult circumstances where the narrative of the last two weeks is that you've got to win by 70 and 60. You don't just need to win, you need to win by massive margins."

Whenever the Women's Rugby League World Cup has featured semi-finals previously, England or Great Britain have always been there. When it has not, they have always finished in the top four.

But this time, they approached the tournament with a different focus, as head coach Staurt Barrow opted for youth over experience.

His squad contained 11 players aged 23 or under, and was largely comprised of players who have full-time occupations away from rugby league.

And that told as England were humbled 78-0 by world champions Australia last Saturday, and found wanting by a Samoa side dominated by NRL Women's Premiership talent. While Australia's domestic league pays its players, money is much tighter in England's Women's Super League.

"Women's Super League has progressed to a certain level and we are bringing young players through so that creeps into the national team," said Barrow.

"It's good and refreshing - but at the same rate we are progressing, it's probably accelerating quicker on this side of the world if I am really honest.

"The investment into the NRLW is not only making the Jillaroos better but it's making all the Pacific nations better as well.

"I think nearly every player for Samoa has played NRLW at some stage and that competition is improving at a rate of knots. We'll have to go back and look at what we can do in our competition.

"We definitely need to do something because the acceleration of the game over here is phenomenal at the moment.

"Back home, we need to have more investment into the women's and girls game. It can't just be a token gesture at some clubs - and I'm not saying it is, but we need to put money into it."

Barrow's other main problem relates to geography and an international calendar that leaves them ill-prepared to face the leading southern hemisphere nations.

Aside from a record 90-4 defeat by Australia in Las Vegas, England's women have been limited to six international fixtures since the previous World Cup, all against France and Wales - in which they have scored 348 points, while conceding four.

"We lost to the better side on the day. I am not going to deny that," Barrow added.

"It was a good game and a good game for England to be in because we have a problem at the moment where we play France or Wales. And no disrespect to those nations but we win them [games] - and we play the Jillaroos and lose heavily.

"This was a nice game to be in where it was competitive all the way. The more of those we can get will definitely help us as a nation."

articles.title: Premier League predictions: Chris Sutton v Bad Day At The Office star John Hannah - & AI
articles.text:
Premier League champions Arsenal endured one of the most embarrassing nights in their history when they were knocked out of the Carabao Cup by League Two side Fleetwood Town on Tuesday, but can they bounce back at Anfield on Sunday?

"Arsenal put a pretty strong team out but were humiliated by Fleetwood, and at Highbury too," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.

"Liverpool seem to be getting it together so this will be a big test for Mikel Arteta's side after the week they have had."

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests.

For week eight, he takes on actor John Hannah, star of new action thriller Bad Day At The Office, who is an Arsenal fan.

Bad Day At The Office will be in UK and Irish cinemas from 30 October.

Do you agree with their predictions? You can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competition.

Hannah, also known for his roles in Four Weddings and a Funeral, Sliding Doors and The Mummy, has been an Arsenal fan since he moved to London from Scotland more than 40 years ago.

As a boy growing up in East Kilbride he had hopes of becoming a footballer long before realising his acting aspirations.

Many of his childhood friends, including Rangers legend Ally McCoist, would go on to forge professional careers.

"I'd like to compare myself to Bukayo Saka," Hannah explained when describing what kind of player he was. "I played on the right wing and I was quite small and fast and I scored a lot of of goals.

"My dream was to be a footballer, and it was all I ever thought about. I played or trained all the time - but, like many dreams, it didn't come true.

"As I got a bit bigger I kind of segued back into midfield but when I discovered women and beer then I kind of stopped playing.

"Once I went to drama school I got very focused on that and then with moving to London and working away, around probably 20 years passed without me kicking a ball.

"But then in 2013 I did a film called Shooting for Socrates, where I played Northern Ireland manager Billy Bingham at the 1986 World Cup.

"We were down in Spain doing some filming there and had a bit of a kickaround and I remember thinking 'yeah, I've still got it you know!'

"Not anymore though - since then I have snapped my ACL [anterior cruciate ligament] which has put paid to football and a lot of sport. It is really just cycling and running for me now."

Chris Sutton and John Hannah were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

Stamford Bridge, 12:30 GMT

Everyone will be watching this game because of Michael Carrick's situation at Manchester United, and wondering how much longer he will be in charge.

Carrick kept his job after the heavy defeats against Como and Bournemouth last week and my view is that, by keeping him on for now, they are possibly just prolonging the misery for him, really.

Going by how insipid United were against Bournemouth, it is hard to see them going to Chelsea and getting anything.

Chelsea were not much better in their defeat by Tottenham last weekend and since then they have been knocked out of the Carabao Cup by Liverpool too.

Xabi Alonso is still without the injured Joao Pedro so I expect Danny Welbeck will lead their attack like he did against Liverpool, and Cole Palmer will be back after his suspension.

Chelsea have had a bad week but I can't see things changing for United, even if Bruno Fernandes is back in their team.

Sutton's prediction: 3-1

John's prediction: With Carrick under pressure, it just feels like Ole Gunnar Solskjaer all over again - he won a few games in a row then they gave him the job and now he doesn't win any. 3-1

AI's prediction: 2-1

Vitality Stadium, 15:00

Bournemouth are flying at the moment, with successive wins over Aston Villa, Manchester United and AC Milan.

Leeds are extremely well structured, however, even if they are not free-scoring this season.

I am sure Daniel Farke would like his team to score more goals, but they don't give away a lot either.

Bournemouth are on a great run but I wonder how much the past week has taken out of them, and that makes me think Leeds could nick a point.

Sutton's prediction: 1-1

John's prediction: This will be a good game, both teams are performing quite well at the moment. 2-2

AI's prediction: 1-1

Gtech Community Stadium, 15:00

Nottingham Forest should have beaten Ipswich last time out but that draw was another example of a game where they haven't taken their chances.

I do think things will turn for Oliver Glasner's side eventually but they are in the bottom three and he is desperate for a win.

I thought Brentford would beat Hull last week but they ended up sharing the points. The Bees do draw a lot of games and that is probably the most sensible prediction here.

Sutton's prediction: 1-1

John's prediction: Brentford at home will maybe give them an edge. 2-1

AI's prediction: 2-1

Coventry Building Society Arena, 15:00

This is big for both teams. It's the battle of the bottom two... and I think Sunderland will win it.

Coventry do not lack any effort and they have got plenty of pace on the counter-attack, but their problem is that they just don't have the quality of most other Premier League teams.

Sunderland got a good win over Brentford in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday night and I am surprised they have been struggling so badly in the league.

The Black Cats are a well-coached team and while I think European football is affecting them in many ways, Brian Brobbey's return from injury is a big positive, and he should help them nick this.

Sutton's prediction: 0-1

John's prediction: I'm surprised by the run Sunderland are on, am still going to put them down for a win here. 0-2

AI's prediction: 1-1

MKM Stadium, 15:00

Both of these promoted teams have got 10 points so far, which shows what decent starts they have made.

I've not picked either of them to get a win yet in my predictions (see table at bottom of page) but that is going to change this week despite the obvious result to go for being a draw.

I could easily make a case for Hull because we know they will give this a real go, but I am actually going to back Ipswich to nick an away win. The Tractor Boys have definitely got a goal or two in them and have already won once on the road, at Crystal Palace.

Sutton's prediction: 1-2

John's prediction: Hull are doing really well. 2-0

AI's prediction: 1-1

Etihad Stadium, 15:00

Manchester City knocked Brighton out of the Carabao Cup on penalties on Wednesday but I don't think we learned too much because both sides made so many changes.

I backed both teams to win last week - and was wrong both times - but I felt City played well against Aston Villa and were a bit unlucky to lose, and the same applied to Brighton in their defeat against Liverpool - they definitely had enough chances to get something from the game.

I am covering this game for Radio 5 Live. There should be some goals in it, and I can see Erling Haaland getting a couple of them.

Sutton's prediction: 3-1

John's prediction: Brighton have really impressed me but I am still going with City at home. 3-1

AI's prediction: 3-1

Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, 17:30

Crystal Palace are through to the Carabao Cup quarter-finals after beating Fulham on Wednesday, and it felt like Eagles boss Pierre Sage needed that result because of his side's poor league form.

Tottenham are on the up at the moment though, and they performed really well in their win at Chelsea even if they did need a bit of luck along the way with Mike Penders punching their first goal into his own net.

However they manage it, the important thing for Spurs is they have found a way of getting results now and I can see them getting another one here.

I do worry for Sage because it seems a lot of Palace fans are uncertain about him and feel his team are too easy to get at.

Because of that, I am going for Spurs to score a couple more goals here.

Sutton's prediction: 2-0

John's prediction: I used to watch Palace a bit when I first moved to London. Spurs have improved but I don't see them winning this one. 0-1

AI's prediction: 2-0

I am not surprised that Fulham's Premier League form has picked up because after watching them earlier in the season I thought they should have more points than they had.

The Cottagers are a well-structured team but I still don't see them stopping an in-form Aston Villa, or their striker Nicolas Jackson, at this moment in time.

Villa are on a great run in the league and I am expecting more goal action from Jackson here.

Sutton's prediction: 3-1

John's prediction: After being a bit up and down, Villa are back at where they were at last season but I have been to see Fulham a few times and my mate is a season-ticket holder there. They have started to kick on too. 0-0

AI's prediction: 2-1

Liverpool proved me wrong against Brighton last week, because they didn't just win, they played well too.

After conceding so many goals last season, you can see they have really tightened things up. Arsenal don't give much away either, so this is going to be very close.

Alexander Isak is scoring goals again for the Reds, and they will be full of confidence coming into this game.

You could make a case for it ending up a repeat of the result we saw at the end of last season, when Dominik Szoboszlai's brilliant free-kick meant Liverpool edged a 1-0 win.

I do think we will see the same scoreline, just with a different winner.

Sutton's prediction: 0-1

John's favourite Arsenal players: Ian Wright, Tony Adams and then Thierry Henry stand out of course but, after that, I was always a big fan of Cesc Fabregas. Santi Cazorla was fantastic too - he was Arsenal through and through - so skilful and so committed.

John's prediction: Liverpool's early form was a bit questionable but they have got better - I am still going to say two-nil to the Arsenal though, because Martin Odegaard will make the difference. 0-2

John's title prediction: I don't actually think we have clicked yet this season and if we find our gear then it is going to be hard to stop us. I don't see anyone other than City putting together a strong challenge.

AI's prediction: 1-2

St James' Park, 20:00

Everton's age-old problem is how Thierno Barry is going to perform because they rely so heavily on how well he is playing up front.

To be fair to David Moyes's side, they carried more of a threat than I expected in their defeat by Arsenal and I can see them getting chances here, because Newcastle are so open.

The Magpies will absolutely go for it again here and I have a sneaky feeling they will leave the door ajar for Everton to pinch the points.

Sutton's prediction: 1-2

John's prediction: Newcastle have been a bit hit and miss. Everton are always pretty solid though. 1-1

AI's prediction: 2-0

Chris got five correct results, including two exact scores, from the 10 games in week eight, giving him a total of 110 points.

That was enough to beat the collective efforts of the BBC readers, who managed four correct results, with two exact scores, for a tally of 100 points.

He also beat both of his guests - Cbeebies star Waffle the Wonder Dog and his owner Simon, played by actor James Merry.

Waffle's three correct results with no exact scores gave him 30 points, while James got four correct results with one exact score for 70 points, meaning they ended up with a average total of 50 points for the BBC predictions league table.

For the fourth week in a row, however, the weekly win went to AI.

It also managed five correct results but with three exact scores, leaving it with 140 points.

There was only one game where everyone picked the right outcome - Arsenal's 2-0 win over Everton - and this time a lot of people got the right scoreline too.

Chris and AI both managed it and so did the BBC readers. From around 28,000 predictions, that was the most popular score selected with more than 11,500 of you getting it exactly right.

articles.title: Rangers v Aberdeen: Can Robinson work Hampden magic in semi-final?
articles.text:
Ten months ago Stephen Robinson could have walked into a Paisley pub and expected a standing ovation and to drink for free all night.

In December the Northern Irishman masterminded St Mirren's second ever League Cup triumph, when his relentless and perfectly drilled side dismantled Celtic.

The pictures in the Hampden dressing room afterwards showed Robinson jumping and singing with his team after reaching the crowning moment of his tenure at the club.

It was an altogether different Robinson which appeared in front of the cameras on Wednesday night, after his Aberdeen side lost at home to Falkirk, the fourth time in six home league games they have failed to score.

Questioned about his future, his answers were short and deflated but he acknowledged patience with his team is wearing thin.

There would be no free drink forthcoming in the Pittodrie Bar for the Aberdeen boss after three wins in 11 to start the Premiership season.

Nonetheless, the arrival of Saturday's Premier Sports Cup semi-final against Rangers represents an opportunity to change the gloomy narrative.

Robinson was more bullish in his media conference on Friday, pointing to his Hampden record and ability to motivate players for big occassions, and he has a point.

As a manager, he is unbeaten in semi-finals at Scotland's national stadium.

He must now channel that to try to upset Rangers and overcome Derek McInnes, a familiar rival who he has bested in cup competitions before.

Last season Robinson's St Mirren knocked out McInnes' title-chasing Hearts, on penalties, in this very competition on their way to lifting the trophy.

When in charge of Motherwell in 2017-18, his team reached both national cup finals, hammering McInnes' Aberdeen 3-0 in the quarter-finals of the League Cup and the semi-finals of the Scottish Cup.

Pedro Caixinha's Rangers were beaten 2-0 in the semi-final of the former that same season.

In the League Cup semi-finals 12 months ago he constructed a gameplan to completely overrun Motherwell. One of the standout sides of last term under the innovative Jens Berthel Askou, the Steelmen were demolished 4-1 at Hampden.

Then came the crowning achievment, the 3-1 final win over Celtic which was as comprehensive a final defeat the serial trophy winners have had at Hampden in over a decade.

Robinson's ability to prevail in a one-off test should not be underestimated, and McInnes said as much this week. Beware of Robinson the underdog.

"I have done it before - every semi or final I have been in the teams that I was with, Motherwell and St Mirren, were not expected to win," Robinson said.

"So I know how to motivate teams, the staff know how to get teams to believe."

Nonetheless the question is whether this Aberdeen team as currently assembled have it in them to produce the type of performance Robinson's teams of the past have put in to claim these notable scalps.

Toughness, organisation, relentless running, and incisive direct attacking at the right times are not qualities this team have shown regularly.

Rather than a clear identity, Robinson has appeared to struggle to know his best team, formation, and approach. Half-time changes and tweaks have been common.

Defensively and at set-pieces the numbers say they have improved on last season, but their creativity and goalscoring has not. And when they have opened up, like against Dundee United a week ago, their defence has suffered.

The absence of defender Mats Knoester in particular is a grievous blow to Aberdeen's hopes of staying resilient in the face of a Rangers team which is unbeaten in 10 games and scoring more goals than when the sides last met at Pittodrie at the end of August.

The frustrated Red Army will be vastly outnumbered at Hampden as they travel south in faint hope of Robinson working his magic in Mount Florida.

If he were to manage it in these cicrumstances, it would not just be another magnificent achievment but a potential turning point in his Aberdeen career.

While Robinson's position has been relentlessly scrutinised, this semi-final is no less important for Rangers boss McInnes.

One league title, one Scottish Cup, and one League Cup in 14 years is an embarrassing trophy return for Rangers given the money the club have spent.

McInnes is the latest manager charged with changing that after two trophyless campaigns at Ibrox, last season being the first under American ownership who have invested heavily.

Despite consistently showing his managerial abilities, in particular when almost winning a sensational title with Hearts last term, McInnes only has one major trophy to show for it.

That was the League Cup he won in 2014 when in charge of Aberdeen, who he led to Hampden regularly, only to come up against Treble-winning Celtic sides at every turn.

Now, though, Rangers' rivals have already been dispatched 3-0 in the quarter-finals, a rousing win at Ibrox which helped change the direction of their season.

Rangers have created the chance for themselves to claim silverware at the first attempt this season - and they simply must take advantage.

"To get the first trophy would be so important, reinforcing confidence, reinforcing belief," the Rangers boss admitted.

"Traditionally, semi-finals can be fraught with a lot of nerves and tension and sometimes they're not the best games, because of what's at stake."

McInnes is leading an expensively assembled but relatively inexperienced team, and at times they were spooked at a raucous Tynecastle on Wednesday as they were fortunate to claim a late draw.

But in the two Old Firm wins this season, they looked physically dominant and completely assured. McInnes needs his team to deal with the occasion again.

A slip now against a struggling Aberdeen will set him and this Rangers team back, and hard-earned trust with fans will disappear.

Win, though, and a December final date against Hearts or Hibernian presents a magnificent opportunity for McInnes to make an early mark at Ibrox.
